articles.title: US Supreme Court again backs Republicans in clash over political ad rates
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commissio...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commission policy that gives party committees access to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates.

The court agreed to ‌let the FCC, which is chaired by Trump ally Brendan Carr, avoid a judicially imposed deadline that would have forced the agency to rule ‌on a Democratic challenge to the policy before the November 3 midterm elections. The FCC joined two Republican committees in filing a request to the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's deadline.

The court ​has a 6-3 conservative majority. Liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated they would have denied the request.

The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, modified its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March in a move seen as a boost to President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans. The president's party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November 3 midterms.

"We are pleased the Supreme Court has granted the FCC's stay request. The court's decision is right on the law and avoids the specter of upending ‌the rules for political ads right in the middle of ⁠an ongoing election," an FCC spokesperson said.

Chief Justice John Roberts had previously lifted the October 9 deadline that was given to the FCC by the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals. The 4th Circuit has accused the FCC of repeated "delay tactics" in ⁠the case, and emphasized the need for an urgent ruling in the Democratic challenge given the looming election.

The Supreme Court's latest action marks the second time in recent weeks that it has addressed the FCC's policy, as major Republican committees head toward the midterms with a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts.

In September, the court granted a request by the national Republican ​committees ​that support the party's candidates in Senate and House of Representatives races to revive the policy ​after the 4th Circuit blocked it. The justices in an ‌8-1 ruling said that the Democratic candidates must wait for the FCC to rule before filing a challenge in court.

The FCC policy at issue requires broadcasters to charge discounted rates for airing certain political advertisements within 60 days of a general election, a window that opened this year on September 4.

A group of Democratic candidates including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in April challenged the policy through in-house proceedings at the FCC. When the agency took no action, the Democrats successfully challenged the policy in the 4th Circuit, a ruling that was later halted by the Supreme Court.

The 4th Circuit on October 7 ordered the FCC to issue a prompt ruling on the ‌Democratic in-house challenge, more than five months after it was filed. In its 2-1 ruling, the ​4th Circuit said its "willingness to tolerate the FCC's delay tactics is at an end."

The Republican committees ​in their Supreme Court filing accused the 4th Circuit of having "short-circuited" the ​FCC's review process.

The Democratic candidates, for their part, accused the FCC in court papers of engaging in "blatant procedural trench warfare to stave ‌off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is ​too late to matter."

The FCC policy gained ​greater significance after the Supreme Court in June struck down federal restrictions on spending coordinated between parties and their candidates, siding with Republican challengers including Vice President JD Vance. Since the June ruling, Republican committees have blown past the former limits ahead of the midterms.

The two Republican committees have exceeded the ​former national caps by more than $48 million, according to Federal ‌Election Commission spending disclosures for July and August. Their Democratic counterparts also eclipsed the former limits, but by much less — just under $4 million.

The three ​main national Republican committees ended August with about $233 million in cash. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $130 million but also carried nearly $18 million in ​debt, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

(Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.title: Watchdog group sues Trump administration over Jared Kushner’s government work
articles.summary: The suit by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington charges that the president’s son-in-law has numerous conflicts of interest.
articles.body:
A watchdog group filed suit Wednesday alleging President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner 's current role as a top envoy for the administration is unlawful and raises numerous conflict-of-interest concerns.

Kushner is wielding tremendous influence internationally "without having been confirmed by the Senate and without having filed a single financial disclosure," the suit by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW , reads.

Kushner "has not been properly vetted for his government role, and he has evaded transparency obligations that aim to ensure he exercises government authority for the good of the American people and not himself," the suit reads.

The suit seeks to have Kushner removed from his position or at least file financial disclosure statements.

Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Jared Kushner, said in a statement that the suit "is without merit."

"Both outside ethics counsel and government ethics attorneys have reviewed Jared Kushner's volunteer government service and confirmed that his arrangements comply with applicable ethics requirements. Jared receives no government salary or compensation, pays his own expenses, and will continue working with counsel to ensure ongoing compliance," Mizelle said.

A White House spokesperson ripped CREW and the suit in a separate statement.

"CREW is an unserious, Trump-deranged organization that has been attacking President Trump, his family, and his administration since the first term. Jared Kushner is a proven dealmaker" with a record of success "that more than speaks for itself," the spokesperson, Anna Kelly, said in a statement.

"His personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements, which he conducts on a volunteer basis at the President's request and while paying his own expenses," the statement said.

The suit mentions numerous overlapping interests in Kushner's diplomatic and business work.

"He represents the United States in the highest profile global conflicts, including the country's efforts to end wars between Israel and Hamas , Ukraine and Russia , and the United States and Iran . He negotiates directly with foreign leaders," the group's filing says.

"Simultaneously, Kushner is also a private businessman . He runs an investment firm with over $6 billion in assets under management. Approximately 99% of those assets are owned by foreign investors, including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The firm holds significant investments abroad, including in Israel," the suit says, all of which "present a heightened risk of financial conflicts of interest."

It adds that "declining a salary and formal title does not change the reality of Kushner's role — he exercises significant executive authority and has done so continuously throughout most of President Trump's second term. And it certainly does not free him from the constitutional constraints of the Appointments Clause or the obligation to file public financial disclosures under the Ethics Act."

The suit seeks to bar Kushner from occupying his government position without Senate confirmation. It says that, if he's a private citizen, "his exercise of government power would violate the private non-delegation doctrine, which prohibits the delegation of government power to private entities."

Despite the scope of Kushner's duties, a White House official said there's nothing unusual about the use of a private envoy.

"The use of private diplomatic envoys to deal with delicate international situations is a presidential practice that dates back to George Washington's presidency," the official said.

articles.title: Midterm campaigns are asking, where's the beef? And how much does it cost?
articles.summary: In the midterm elections, meat is on the menu.As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war, they also are having a food fight over wh...
articles.body:
In the midterm elections , meat is on the menu.

As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war , they also are having a food fight over who is the most red-blooded carnivore.

The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, "you know you have so many proteins to choose from."

The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, "Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead."

The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it is the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they are culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough.

In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democrat James Talarico, the current U.S. Senate nominee, boasted that his campaign at the time for the Texas Statehouse was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he is not a real Texan.

In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed.

Rutinel, 31, is now running against Gabe Evans, the Republican who represents Colorado's 8th Congressional District. The vast swath in the northeastern part of the state is dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat "as little as possible."

Rutinel has made a point of publicly eating steak tacos during the campaign and is backed by the meatpackers' union. "I don't think Coloradans care about what's on my plate," he said in an interview after a recent campaign stop. "I think they care more about being able to afford what's on theirs."

Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel's meal preferences. "I don't care what he eats personally," Evans said in an interview. "I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way."

High-stakes role for meat in the debate over rising consumer prices

Republicans, in the same way, have gone after two other Democrats running for the U.S. House. They are hammering Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd District, an area filled with hog farms, over a 2020 Facebook post supporting "meatless May," and Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st District for his long-standing vegetarianism and animal rights activism.

Also in Iowa, Republican U.S. Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. "He'd rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms," the congresswoman said at a campaign appearance.

Democrats have spotlighted meat as well, but mainly as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters' pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally.

Those moves, however, have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office.

That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former Mississippi agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom's video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the "pick another senator" line in the spot — is running a long-shot challenge in Mississippi.

A spokesman for Hyde-Smith's campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. "It is Scott Colom who supports Biden-era policies that drove up inflation," said Nathan Calvert.

Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

This story has been corrected to reflect that Manny Rutinel, a congressional candidate in Colorado, said in an interview, "I think they care more about being able to afford what's on theirs," rather than, "I think they care more about what's on theirs."

articles.title: Por que Helder Barbalho não conseguiu eleger Hana Ghassan no Pará | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-governador garantiu vaga em Brasília e ajudou a eleger aliado ao Congresso Nacional, mas viu sucessora perder a disputa pelo governo para Dr. Daniel (Podemos), ex-aliado que se consolidou como principal polo do “antibarbalismo”.
articles.summary: Ex-governador garantiu uma vaga em Brasília e ajudou a eleger um aliado ao Congresso Nacional, mas viu sua sucessora perder a disputa pelo governo para Dr. Daniel (Podemos).
articles.body:
A eleição para o governo do Pará em 2026 deixou uma contradição no tabuleiro político do estado: enquanto o ex-governador Helder Barbalho ( MDB ) demonstrou força ao se eleger senador e ainda puxar o aliado Chicão ( União Brasil ) para a 2ª vaga em Brasília, o seu projeto de continuidade no Palácio do Governo sofreu uma reviravolta.

A atual governadora e ex-candidata à reeleição, Hana Ghassan (MDB), que assumiu o cargo após a saída de Helder para disputar o Senado, foi derrotada ainda no 1º turno por Dr. Daniel Santos ( Podemos ). Com 97,46% das urnas apuradas, o ex-prefeito de Ananindeua foi eleito com 2.303.759 votos (51,75%), mais de 250 mil votos à frente da emedebista, que tinha 2.052.759 votos (46,11%).

A derrota de Hana expõe um desafio para o grupo de Helder Barbalho: o tamanho da força política de um líder não garante, por si só, a eleição de seu sucessor.

O g1 ouviu especialistas para identificar os principais fatores que contribuíram para a derrota de Hana. Entre os motivos estão:

Eleitorado nas grandes cidades: a força da estrutura política e dos aliados locais construída por Helder manteve-se nos municípios menores, onde Hana venceu na maioria , mas o eleitorado dos grandes colégios eleitorais optou majoritariamente por Dr. Daniel.

Dificuldade de construir identidade própria: Hana assumiu o governo em abril de 2026 e teve um período curto para se apresentar ao eleitorado com autonomia.

Ascensão de Dr. Daniel como "antibarbalista": ex-prefeito de Ananindeua se consolidou como polo antagonista e pautou debates centrais na campanha.

Possível erro de estratégia na aliança nacional: apesar de fazer parte da aliança de Lula e receber o apoio público do presidente, Hana teve pouca associação visual e política com o presidente durante a campanha, segundo os analistas. Enquanto isso, Daniel se aproximou de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) .

Desgaste político e busca por alternância: a permanência do mesmo grupo político no poder por quase 10 anos gerou um desgaste natural, alimentando a percepção de concentração de poder.

À esquerda, Hana Ghassan e Helder Barbalho; à direita, Dr Daniel Santos. — Foto: Ascom Hana Ghassan / Ascom Ananindeua

Embora a eleição para o governo do Pará tenha sido decidida ainda no 1º turno, a movimentação política de Dr. Daniel no estado continua. Na segunda (19), ele deve participar de um evento com Flávio em Marabá, numa tentativa de reforçar o palanque do candidato em um estado onde Lula foi o mais votado no 1º turno.

Em outra frente, Helder Barbalho segue reafirmando o apoio a Lula na disputa presidencial: “Respeito as posições divergentes, mas faço questão de deixar clara a minha”, afirmou em uma publicação nas redes sociais.

Já Hana Ghassan segue à frente do governo do Pará até dia 31 de dezembro. Após a derrota, a governadora afirmou na quinta (15) que pretende conduzir a transição para a próxima administração de forma "democrática, pacífica e transparente".

Do 'palanque' no interior às urnas das grandes cidades

Dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) mostram que Hana Ghassan saiu vitoriosa na maioria dos 144 municípios paraenses, vencendo em 80 deles (locais com menos eleitores). No entanto, Dr. Daniel obteve desempenhos melhores nos grandes colégios eleitorais do estado, como Belém e Ananindeua, cidades da região metropolitana.

Analistas explicam que há um comportamento eleitoral diferente entre interior e centros urbanos. Nos municípios menores, predomina a força do "palanque tradicional" , que são acordos políticos com prefeitos, vereadores e lideranças regionais. Já nas grandes cidades, o eleitorado é mais influenciado pelo debate público, redes sociais, exposição midiática e queixas sobre serviços públicos.

Para o professor Gustavo Ribeiro (UFPA), esse desenho geográfico revela a diferença entre a força do "palanque tradicional" e a autonomia do eleitorado urbano.

"O que o ex-governador Helder Barbalho conseguiu fazer foi organizar uma grande base de apoio ao seu governo, que continuou no período da Hana. A construção do palanque se manteve firme nas menores cidades. Mas você tem um eleitorado nas maiores cidades que tende a ter uma certa independência das disputas locais ", analisa Ribeiro.

Em Ananindeua, segunda maior cidade do estado, Daniel teve avaliação positiva sobre a gestão municipal, o que, segundo os analistas, também pode ter influenciado na vitória dele nas cidades da região metropolitana de Belém.

Diferentemente de outros nomes apoiados por Helder Barbalho em pleitos recentes, como Igor Normando na Prefeitura de Belém ou Chicão na disputa ao Senado, Hana Ghassan enfrentou a necessidade de construir uma "marca própria" durante a campanha eleitoral .

Primo do ex-governador, Normando, por exemplo, era secretário de Articulação da Cidadania (SEAC) no governo Helder antes de se tornar candidato a prefeito. Ele tinha como principal marca da gestão e da campanha em 2024 as Usinas da Paz , locais importantes que abrigam serviços gratuitos de lazer, esporte e capacitação profissional para a população em bairros da periferia. Foi eleito com 56,38% dos votos , vencendo Eder Mauro (PL).

Já Hana ocupou, enquanto vice-governadora, posições de destaque na gestão estadual, como a presidência do Comitê da COP 30 , conferência global realizada em novembro de 2025 em Belém, e assumido o governo em abril de 2026 após a desincompatibilização de Helder, mas ainda precisava se apresentar ao grande público .

"Há uma diferença bem específica entre alguém como Chicão ou Igor Normando e a governadora Hana. Chicão e Igor tinham marcas políticas próprias já dadas, que puderam acrescentar à campanha. No caso de Hana, o apoio não contou com esse aspecto . É diferente você ter que apresentar a candidata, construir a reputação pública do ponto de vista do eleitorado e fazê-la ganhar a sucessão. É mais difícil", explica Gustavo Ribeiro.

O cientista político Rodolfo Marques também aponta dificuldades na consolidação de uma identidade eleitoral. Ele destaca quatro fatores: a dificuldade de construir identidade política própria; desgaste "natural" de um grupo político no poder há quase 10 anos; a capacidade de Daniel apresentar "alternativa competitiva"; e a articulação da direita para vencer o "barbalismo".

"Hana assumiu o governo em abril de 2026 e teve um período curto para se apresentar ao eleitorado como uma liderança capaz de comandar o Estado com relativa autonomia", afirma.

De aliado interno ao polo do 'antibarbalismo'

Conhecido pelo perfil pragmático, Helder construiu hegemonia ampla e diversa no Pará, abrigando na base aliada partidos e lideranças da esquerda, do centro e da direita. Mas, na ciência política, cenários de forte concentração de poder costumam gerar tendência à bipolarização.

"O governo Helder e seu grupo político se estabeleceram como um grande polo da política paraense. Estava faltando aparecer o polo antagonista que, pela dinâmica do sistema, iria aparecer em algum momento. E o Dr. Daniel se mostrou mais competente para se apresentar em relação a isso. Ele se consolidou como o antibarbalismo", afirma o professor Gustavo Ribeiro.

É aí que entra a trajetória de Dr. Daniel Santos. Médico de 40 anos, ele começou a carreira no próprio grupo de Helder. Foi deputado estadual presidente da Alepa e se elegeu prefeito de Ananindeua em 2020 com apoio direto de Barbalho.

Dr. Daniel e Helder Barbalho: de aliados a adversários — Foto: Arte g1

"A trajetória do Daniel é um dos aspectos mais interessantes dessa eleição. Mostra como uma liderança que emerge dentro de uma determinada coalizão pode construir a própria autonomia. Ele rompeu com o grupo do Helder e passou a ocupar um espaço de oposição que tinha condições de ampliar, porque já conhecia a dinâmica política", pontua Rodolfo Marques.

" Daniel acabou construindo um polo de reorganização da oposição paraense", diz Marques.

Pauta da oposição e erro na aliança nacional

Além de articular o apoio de setores da direita, do agronegócio e de simpatizantes do bolsonarismo, Dr. Daniel conseguiu levar para o centro da campanha temas que atingiam diretamente a gestão de Helder.

Entre os principais pontos explorados na campanha estiveram as críticas à concessão do abastecimento de água (Águas do Pará) e à cobrança de pedágios nas rodovias estaduais - ambas políticas implementadas no governo de Helder.

Especialistas também apontam um "erro estratégico" na campanha governista quanto ao uso de alianças nacionais.

Embora Lula tenha sido o candidato à Presidência mais votado no Pará , Hana teve pouca associação visual e política com o presidente durante a campanha, segundo os analistas. Uma das poucas exceções foi um comício na Praça da República , em Belém, em que Hana reforçou a parceria entre Lula e Helder; e o apoio de Lula à candidatura dela.

" A governadora Hana colocou todos os ovos na caçamba do apoio do ex-governador Helder Barbalho. Houve um erro estratégico tremendo para um estado no qual o presidente Lula obteve mais votos do que o eleitorado de oposição: ela não tentou se acercar mais da campanha do presidente Lula ", analisa Gustavo Ribeiro.

"Se tivesse conseguido trazer mais do eleitorado de Lula, o resultado poderia ter sido diferente", ele complementa.

Apesar do revés no Palácio do Governo, analistas ponderam que o resultado das urnas não significa a derrocada definitiva da influência dos Barbalho no Pará, mas demonstra os limites da transferência automática de votos.

"Eu não interpreto o resultado como uma rejeição ao Helder Barbalho, mas como um sinal de que o capital político, seja ele de quem for, tem seus próprios limites", conclui Rodolfo Marques.

Dr. Daniel assume o Governo do Pará em 6 de janeiro de 2027, tendo como vice Ellayne de Almeida (Podemos), liderança conservadora na região do oeste do estado. Entre os primeiros atos anunciados está a rescisão do contrato de concessão do saneamento no estado .

articles.title: Mais de 4,3 mil seções eleitorais mudaram de local para o 2º turno; veja como consultar onde votar | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o TSE, mudanças atingem 0,87% das 499 mil seções do país e ocorreram por motivos como chuvas, reformas, problemas de acessibilidade e falta de energia. Eleitor deve conferir endereço antes de votar.
articles.summary: Segundo o TSE, mudanças atingem 0,87% das 499 mil seções do país e ocorreram por motivos como chuvas, reformas, problemas de acessibilidade e falta de energia. Eleitor deve conferir endereço antes de votar.
articles.body:
A Justiça Eleitoral mudou o local de votação de 4.352 seções eleitorais para o segundo turno das eleições de 2026, marcado para domingo, 25 de outubro . O número corresponde a 0,87% das 499.248 seções instaladas no país.

Segundo o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), as alterações foram feitas por motivos como fortes chuvas, reformas de última hora, problemas na acessibilidade dos prédios e falta de energia elétrica.

Em algumas situações, locais danificados tiveram as seções transferidas preventivamente para prédios próximos considerados mais seguros.

Por isso, mesmo quem votou normalmente no primeiro turno d eve conferir novamente o endereço antes de sair de casa ( entenda mais abaixo ) .

A consulta pode ser feita pelo aplicativo e-Título ou pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral , no site do TSE. Segundo o tribunal, mudanças feitas pelos cartórios eleitorais aparecem imediatamente nesses canais.

Dados divulgados pelo TSE nesta sexta-feira (16) mostram que as alterações se concentraram em alguns dos estados com os maiores eleitorados. São Paulo teve 982 seções com mudança de local; Minas Gerais, 514; Rio de Janeiro, 431; e Bahia, 312.

O tribunal afirma que a troca de endereço não significa que houve redução no número de seções eleitorais nem prejuízo aos eleitores.

Urnas sendo preparadas para o 2º turno em São José dos Campos. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

Entre os motivos para as alterações estão eventos climáticos que comprometeram imóveis utilizados pela Justiça Eleitoral.

Em Confresa, no interior de Mato Grosso, por exemplo, fortes chuvas e ventos registrados nos dias 9 e 10 de outubro danificaram a cobertura de uma escola municipal que funcionava como local de votação. O imóvel apresentou infiltrações e problemas nos forros.

Um laudo de engenharia emitido no domingo (11) recomendou a interdição preventiva imediata da escola. Com isso, as seções eleitorais instaladas ali foram transferidas para outro endereço nas proximidades.

Além de fenômenos climáticos, segundo o TSE, também levaram a mudanças manutenções de última hora, reformas não concluídas em escolas e perda das condições mínimas de acessibilidade ou de fornecimento de energia elétrica.

As alterações não são determinadas diretamente pelo TSE. Segundo o tribunal, a decisão cabe a cada zona eleitoral, que analisa as condições dos locais de votação e a infraestrutura disponível no município.

Em resposta à TV Globo , o TSE também informou que mudanças entre os dois turnos podem ocorrer em razão de eventos extremos, como alagamentos, temporais e outras condições climáticas que causem danos aos locais de votação.

O tribunal orientou que as situações específicas de cada estado fossem verificadas junto aos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais (TREs).

O segundo turno será realizado no próximo domingo (25), das 8h às 17h, pelo horário de Brasília . Na disputa pela Presidência da República estão Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Além da eleição presidencial, haverá segundo turno para governador em seis estados e no Distrito Federal.

Como haverá menos cargos em disputa nesta etapa, o TSE afirma que a votação deverá ser mais rápida e que a expectativa é de filas menores e maior agilidade no atendimento.

Antes da confirmação das 4.352 seções tiveram esse alteração, a Justiça Eleitoral orientava ao eleitor que ele deveria comparecer ao mesmo local e seção do primeiro turno, exceto quando houvesse alteração excepcional pelo órgão, recomendando a consulta aos canais oficiais.

Neste ano, o presidente do TSE, ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, criou a Sala Nacional de Situação Climática para as Eleições 2026, destinada a acompanhar possíveis impactos de fenômenos climáticos na realização da votação.

Segundo o tribunal, o monitoramento é feito em conjunto com órgãos como o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet), o Centro Nacional de Monitoramento e Alertas de Desastres Naturais (Cemaden), o Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), a Agência Nacional de Águas e Saneamento Básico (ANA), a Defesa Civil e as Forças Armadas.

A rede acompanha situações como tempestades, secas e desastres naturais que possam afetar locais de votação ou rotas de transporte.

articles.title: Quem é Deputa Mané Buchada, influenciador eleito como deputado estadual da PB entre os mais votados | G1
articles.standfirst: Manoel Filgueira, o "Deputa Mané Buchada", foi eleito como deputado estadual com 53.641 votos, sendo o 6º mais votado na Paraíba. Ele tem mais de 2 milhões de seguidores nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: Manoel Filgueira, o "Deputa Mané Buchada", foi eleito como deputado estadual com 53.641 votos, sendo o 6º mais votado na Paraíba. Ele tem mais de 2 milhões de seguidores nas redes sociais.
articles.body:
Quem é 'Deputa Mané Buchada', humorista eleito como deputado estadual da PB entre os mais votados — Foto: Redes sociais

O influenciador Manoel Batista Filgueira Neto, de 36 anos, foi eleito para o cargo de deputado estadual da Paraíba, entre os mais votados, no pleito de 4 de outubro. Conhecido nas redes sociais como Deputa Mané Buchada e foi o 6º mais votado nas Eleições 2026 para a Assembleia Legislativa da Paraíba (ALPB).

Ele foi eleito com 53.641 votos pelo Partido Liberal (PL). Com mais de 2 milhões de seguidores nas redes sociais, Deputa ganhou popularidade com seus conteúdos na internet e agora se prepara para assumir um mandato no Legislativo estadual, a partir de 2027.

Segundo o deputado eleito, a atuação dele na Assembleia deve ser pautada em temas como saúde, educação e segurança alimentar.

Deputa Mané Buchada é o nome do personagem humorístico criado por Manoel Batista Filgueira. O personagem faz uma sátira com os próprios políticos. Os vídeos publicados nas redes sociais consistem na figura em ocasiões de críticas ao descaso do poder público, como vias esburacadas.

Em um vídeo, por exemplo, o Deputa Mané Buchada aparece em uma rodovia com um buraco cheio de água, vestido de terno, e com uma venda nos olhos, com "eles não conseguem ver a realidade", escrito na legenda.

Sobre o nome escolhido para o personagem, ele explicou como surgiu. Ele disse que contou com a ajuda da filha.

"Foi de forma muito simples, gravando nosso conteúdo de fiscalização através do entretenimento, em algum momento a gente escreveu um roteiro e disse 'Deputa'. Eu pedi para Aslen, a minha filha, ela citar 'Deputa', isso soa de uma forma muito divertida para o público que assistia. E nos próximos vídeos ficou 'Deputa'. O Mané Buchada foi de antes, de outros vídeos que a gente fazia", explicou em entrevista à Rádio CBN Paraíba.

Em relação a como prefere ser chamado após a eleição na ALPB, ele disse que a escolha vai ser do povo e que não tem preferências.

Manoel Filgueira disse também que os conteúdos produzidos por ele são "denúncias" feitas através de "ironias". E que a linguagem dos vídeos nas redes sociais "conscientizou pessoas". Ele avaliou que isso se refletiu na votação para a Assembleia.

Eleito pelo PL, que fez seis cadeiras para a nova legislatura na ALPB, Deputa Mané Buchada reconheceu que está dentro do "bloco do PL". Ele disse que vai permanecer com um trabalho de "conscientização" sobre temas como saúde, educação e segurança pública.

"Tem essa cultura à nível não só estadual, mas Federal, municipal. De fato, as pessoas não se importam mais se vai abandonar ou se vai dar continuidade, as pessoas sofrem caladas. A gente faz esse trabalho de conscientização e vê que tá dando resultado, pelo menos na Paraíba. Então vamos continuar com esse trabalho de fiscalização para as pessoas se inteirarem para onde vai o dinheiro público e cada ação feita", disse.

Na entrevista para a CBN, ele disse ter um "hall" de propostas para segurança alimentar, merenda e outras á.

Uma dos primeiros compromissos de Deputa Mané Buchada na Assembleia será a escolha do novo presidente da Casa. Ele disse na entrevista que, apesar de fazer parte do PL, vai votar de forma independente.

"Todos ligaram para mim, mas de forma cordial, parabenizando pela vitória. Para mim é tudo muito novo, estou correndo contra o tempo para aprender e tentando conhecer o máximo possível quem estará como candidato, para escolher o melhor para o povo paraibano. Estou blocado, mas cada um com sua postura independente. Se a decisão for parecida, foi coincidência. Não vou votar porque alguém indicou", disse Deputa.

O deputado e os outros eleitos assumem as cadeiras na AL a partir de 2027.

articles.title:
Ministério da Justiça pede que ANPD investigue se Meta descumpriu Marco Civil da Internet
  | G1
articles.standfirst: Medida ocorre após a pasta receber relatos de que plataforma tem feito bloqueios e restrições de conteúdo sem explicar qual regra o usuário descumpriu.
articles.summary: Medida ocorre após a pasta receber relatos de que plataforma tem feito bloqueios e restrições de conteúdo sem explicar qual regra o usuário descumpriu.
articles.body:
Logo da Meta, empresa dona do Instagram e Facebook. — Foto: Tony Avelar/AP

O Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP) pediu que a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) investigue se a Meta, responsável pelo Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp, está descumprindo o Marco Civil da Internet.

A medida ocorre após a pasta receber relatos de que a plataforma tem feito bloqueios e restrições de conteúdo sem explicar qual regra o usuário descumpriu. O MJ também encaminhou as informações ao Ministério Público Federal (MPF).

Em uma das notas técnicas, a pasta reúne relatos encaminhados por diferentes organizações da sociedade civil. A CTRL+Z, por exemplo, contabilizou 1.121 relatos entre 25 de setembro e 13 de outubro, envolvendo casos de supressão de alcance e restrições de funcionalidades. Já o Observatório de Olho na Censura documenta casos desde janeiro de 2026.

Segundo os técnicos, os relatos indicam seis falhas: decisões sem motivação e sem recurso, enquadramento sem leitura do contexto, remoções após denúncias em massa, cortes de alcance sem comunicação, aprovação de anúncios pagos do exterior com deepfakes e desinformação, e respostas insuficientes às autoridades.

Para a Secretaria Nacional de Direitos Digitais, órgão vinculado ao MJ, os relatos podem configurar descumprimento de obrigações previstas no Marco Civil da Internet, em vigor desde julho deste ano.

A norma estabelece, entre outros deveres, a comunicação e a fundamentação das decisões de moderação, a possibilidade de contestação pelo usuário, a análise do contexto antes da indisponibilização de conteúdo e medidas para coibir o uso abusivo de notificações.

Diante disso, o Ministério da Justiça pediu que a agência cobre informações à Meta sobre "as regras e procedimentos de moderação e de gestão de reclamações, os relatórios de transparência, os registros dos casos relatados, os critérios e registros de redução de alcance, os mecanismos contra denúncias coordenadas, os procedimentos de verificação de anunciantes".

Em paralelo, também foi solicitado auditoria nos sistemas automatizados de moderação, classificação e distribuição da empresa.

A pasta sugere, ainda, que a ANPD avalie a adoção de medida cautelar ou preventiva diante da proximidade do segundo turno, em 25 de outubro.

Entre as medidas estão a preservação de registros, a revisão de restrições aplicadas sem justificativa comunicada ao usuário e a exigência de revisão humana e fundamentação em casos envolvendo veículos jornalísticos, organizações da sociedade civil, movimentos sociais, entidades estudantis e conteúdos político-eleitorais.

articles.title: La principal revista política de EEUU elogia a España por su Alta Velocidad y dicta sentencia: "Hay motivos para creer que es posible"
articles.standfirst: Un análisis estadounidense destaca a España como referente mundial en infraestructura ferroviaria eficiente
articles.summary: Un análisis estadounidense destaca a España como referente mundial en infraestructura ferroviaria eficiente
articles.body: Estados Unidos sufre algunos de los costes de infraestructura de transporte más elevados del planeta. El metro de la Segunda Avenida de Nueva York se construyó a "un costo exorbitante de 2.500 millones de dólares por milla", mientras que la línea de alta velocidad de California supera los "200 millones de dólares por milla", cuadruplicando la media internacional y multiplicando por diez los costes de construcción en España. Esta espiral presupuestaria frena proyectos en todo el país. Según detalla el influyente análisis de Marc J. Dunkelman para una de las principales revistas políticas que se publica de manera trimestral 'American Affairs', la gobernanza estadounidense sufre un choque permanente: el impulso de centralizar el poder para lograr objetivos contrasta con el deseo de fragmentarlo. Desde la década de 1960, la dispersión democrática y la proliferación de normativas ambientales han otorgado a los ciudadanos herramientas para "ralentizar, detener o desviar proyectos". Los litigios y las exigencias locales disparan la factura de forma sistemática. En el metro de Washington, la presión ciudadana obligó a introducir modificaciones constantes que elevaron el coste total hasta los "10.000 millones de dólares, en lugar de los 2.500 millones previstos inicialmente". Como advirtió la ingeniería del proyecto, "no hay manera de construir un proyecto de obras públicas tan gigantesco como el Metro con un presupuesto razonable y teniendo en cuenta todas las influencias externas". En el proyecto ferroviario californiano se repite la misma parálisis por decenas de demandas judiciales. La legislación local ha servido de freno constante, obligando a sufragar indemnizaciones millonarias que van desde "500 000 dólares a una iglesia" hasta costosos desvíos urbanos, retrasando los plazos y vaciando el presupuesto público en interminables negociaciones de terceros. Frente a este modelo de bloqueo institucional, las agencias que ejecutan obras de bajo coste operan con autoridad centralizada. En España, las líneas de metro madrileñas costaron una fracción mínima de los estándares neoyorquinos y la construcción pública "está exenta de muchos de los problemas de autoridad que dificultan los proyectos en Estados Unidos". La normativa española dota a la Administradora de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias (ADIF) de competencias directas para anular trabas urbanísticas locales. Además, los estudios de impacto ambiental no paralizan la construcción y "es improbable que los tribunales concedan medidas cautelares contra proyectos de infraestructura aprobados", evitando el colapso judicial estadounidense. El contraste demuestra que la ejecución eficaz de una gran obra pública requiere un control férreo sobre el diseño y la ejecución. Cuando la burocracia se fragmenta y el poder se erosiona, la gestión se vuelve inviable; por el contrario, el éxito de la alta velocidad española demuestra que "hay motivos para creer que es posible" construir con eficiencia y rigor presupuestario.

articles.title: Army expo attendees skeptical of Trump's Iran peace deal hopes: 'Beat 'em into submission'
articles.summary: AUSA Exposition attendees question Trump's optimism about an Iran deal, arguing military and economic sanctions must intensify before Tehran talks.
articles.body: Attendees at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Exposition were skeptical of President Donald Trump’s signal that a deal with Iran to end the war may be near, arguing the United States needs to continue its military and economic pressure on Tehran to bring the conflict to a close. "Look at history, and that area only respects strength, right?" a member of AUSA’s Marne chapter in Georgia told Fox News Digital about Iran. "We're not going to get a deal with them. We're going to have to, unfortunately, beat them into submission." He added, "There is no such thing as negotiation. So I think we're probably looking at at least another year, if not two." TRUMP AGAIN SAYS DEAL IS CLOSE, THEN CONFIRMS A LAST-MINUTE AGREEMENT WITH IRAN, BUT DETAILS STILL SECRET The war began in February with joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. The conflict has continued despite an April ceasefire and a June agreement intended to pave the way for a broader settlement, which later collapsed amid renewed fighting. Trump still signals optimism about ending the conflict, saying earlier this month that Iran was "ready to fold up" and suggesting the war could end before the November midterm elections. "It looks like you guys are holding off because of the midterms," Lincoln from Australia said. He also argued that wealthy Gulf allies should take greater responsibility for their own security. "But it also appears that the Gulf allies need to step up and start doing something for themselves, for their own defense," Lincoln said. "Saudi Arabia doesn't seem to be doing enough." "It shouldn't just be the United States providing security for the entire world," he added. TRUMP’S IRAN DEAL REACHES MAKE-OR-BREAK DEADLINE AS 60-DAY NEGOTIATING CLOCK EXPIRES Trump said Thursday that he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran after reports started circulating that the Department of War was developing new strike plans that could include using a bomb known as the "Mother of All Bombs" against Iranian nuclear sites and energy infrastructure. "I know they tried diplomatic channels and … that's a good idea," Joe from Florida said. "It looks like we have to move beyond that. It looks like force is needed. They keep trying force on us. Let's talk their language." An Army veteran had more optimism toward the prospects of a deal, arguing that continued economic pressure on Iran could help to end the conflict. "Physically, they're having a hard time because there's a lot of pressure on them," Carl from Maryland said. "They're running low on resources, cash." US ECONOMIC CHOKEHOLD ON IRAN REACHES PEAK LEVERAGE AS COLLAPSE RISKS EMERGE He continued, "I think that more of … this continued pressure on them — economically, the sanctions — not allowing them to export the oil that they've done in the past to their other partners will continue to put pressure on them to cease hostilities." But even among those who expressed support for Trump's handling of the conflict, questions remained about whether the Trump administration could end the conflict through negotiations. "I think he'll do what he can, it's best for our country, but I'm very skeptical that there's any type of brokered peace between us and Iran."

articles.title: Ilhan Omar raid sparks ominous prediction from watchdog: 'They probably got the goods'
articles.summary: Oversight Project's Mike Howell warns Ilhan Omar's HSI raid signals deeper congressional accountability failures and predicts more revelations ahead.
articles.body: The federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home prompted warnings Wednesday from a conservative watchdog leader that more revelations could be coming, as the Minnesota Democrat faces separate investigations involving her immigration records and financial disclosures. Oversight Project President Mike Howell, whose group pushed to strip a $1.031 million earmark backed by Omar, says the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) search raises broader questions about congressional accountability and what investigators may uncover next. His warning comes as U.S. Attorney Jeanine F. Pirro confirmed on "America Reports" that her office is investigating the Minnesota Democrat's financial disclosures, while separate reporting revealed that federal investigators had subpoenaed Omar's relatives as part of an immigration-related probe. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION "I think there's other shoes that are going to drop here," Howell told Fox News Digital. "That's why I think the Democrats really just couldn't resist the temptation to jump out of this before they saw any evidence and just circle the wagons [around Omar]," he said. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ "I will say it appears they're walking that back a little bit. It has shifted from just a wholesale defense of Omar to a non-substantive defense, talking about, ‘well, this stuff was old,’ or ‘this is political since she's Ilhan Omar’." Howell suggested that Omar’s defenders’ arguments indicate that it’s "not all peaches and cream underneath the hood." WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION Howell's warning extends beyond Omar to what he describes as a broader failure of accountability in Washington, where lawmakers can champion taxpayer-funded projects that later face questions about their legitimacy. Fox News has learned that federal investigators are examining whether Omar's age was accurately reported when she arrived in the United States in 1995 and when she acquired U.S. citizenship in 2000, including whether any inaccurate information could have affected her eligibility for citizenship through her father under the law in effect at the time. ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION The inquiry also encompasses paperwork completed by her late father and whether he provided inaccurate information. Sources told Fox News that investigators are examining potential immigration fraud spanning multiple years. Federal investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas as part of the immigration inquiry, including subpoenas to members of Omar's family. The immigration inquiry is separate from the financial-disclosure investigation being handled by Pirro, sources told Fox News. "We're in the speculation zone, of course," Howell told Fox News Digital, acknowledging uncertainty about the full scope of the federal investigations. DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS Still, Howell argued that obtaining a search warrant for a sitting member of Congress in Washington suggested investigators had developed substantial evidence, though the warrant establishes only that a judge found probable cause to believe the search would uncover evidence or other items subject to seizure, not that Omar committed a crime. Howell pointed to what he viewed as a unique combination of circumstances — an HSI investigation under the Trump administration, a warrant authorized by a federal judge in heavily Democratic Washington, D.C., and the proximity of the election — as reasons he believes investigators may have substantial evidence. "They probably got the goods on her," Howell said. "You don't get a federal judge to sign off on something like this in Washington, D.C., of all places, unless there is something that is rather convincing." Jonathan Fahey, a former acting ICE director and federal prosecutor in the neighboring Eastern District of Virginia, said the timing of the HSI search raises questions about whether investigators are examining more recent documents tied to longstanding immigration allegations. "I surmise that what they may be looking for is newer things that were used with what they believe is false information," Fahey told Fox News Digital, referring to the immigration investigation. Fahey suggested that knowingly repeating materially false information in more recent federal filings could create separate legal exposure, depending on the documents, circumstances and applicable statutes, even if criminal charges based solely on older paperwork would be barred by the statute of limitations. Former FBI agent Nicole Parker cautioned that Omar might not face criminal liability if her father completed allegedly false paperwork while she was a minor. "If her father lied and filled out the [citizenship/naturalization] forms, then in my opinion, she will not be criminally held responsible," Parker said. However, Parker said Omar could face a separate legal question if authorities establish she obtained citizenship through materially-false information. "It could potentially cause her to be denaturalized and lose her citizenship if her citizenship was gained on false pretenses and false information," she said. In January, the Oversight Project challenged a proposed $1.031 million earmark for Generation Hope MN's Justice Empowerment Initiative in Minneapolis, a project backed by Omar and Minnesota's Democratic senators. The group raised concerns about the nonprofit's finances, operations and eligibility for taxpayer funding, including questions about its addiction recovery services at a location shared with a Minneapolis restaurant, whose owner previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Generation Hope operated in upstairs office space. "We said, let's go check out those earmarks," Howell recalled. Conservative Republicans subsequently objected to the funding, with Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, among those pushing for its removal. The earmark was stripped, and Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, later requested Justice Department scrutiny of the nonprofit. The funding dispute raised questions about congressional vetting of proposed recipients, but its removal did not establish fraud by Omar or the organization. No connection between the earmark controversy and either federal investigation has been publicly confirmed. As part of his broader "institutional rot" argument, Howell argued that Omar’s earmark controversy is not unique, criticizing what he sees as lawmakers placing loyalties outside the United States ahead of their constitutional responsibilities. "This isn't normal. And it only seems normal because it's been happening so much. And I think it's about time we take the oath to the Constitution that members swear seriously," he said. Her office called the search an abuse of power and previously pointed to congressional ethics findings recommending dismissal of allegations concerning her financial disclosures, but did not respond to a request for comment on this story. articles.title: Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners
articles.summary: Can the United States reassert influence with pragmatic, transactional approach to Central Asia?
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Samarkand, the fabled Silk Road city in what is now central Uzbekistan, for talks with key regional ministers on Saturday.

The C5+1 – Central Asia plus the US – summit to be held from Saturday to Tuesday heralds Washington’s new approach to the ex-Soviet region – pragmatic, purely transactional and devoid of speeches about democratisation and human rights.

At the dawn of Central Asia’s independence, Americans used to show up in the mostly Muslim region strategically stretched between Russia, China and Iran, bearing gifts – and giving lectures.

After the 1991 Soviet collapse, amid the region’s economic degradation, joblessness and poverty, US and European diplomats and businessmen were seen as ambassadors of the brave new world of capitalist prosperity.

They wanted reforms – and not just the economic ones.

Western diplomats made sure that former Communist apparatchiks-turned-new regional leaders understood that they’d get investments, technologies and international recognition only in exchange for abandoning the Soviet-era totalitarian ways of governing and building the economy.

The West held forums and workshops on human rights, democracy and decentralisation of governance, and sent thousands of students and officials to Western schools.

And the West accused regional leaders of losing their moral compass and threatened sanctions when they began to amend their nation’s constitutions to extend their presidential terms, appoint their family members and friends to key government jobs and help them create business empires that often competed with Western investors.

“When the West began moralising, teaching them about democracy, human rights, they immediately turned towards China or Russia,” Galiya Ibragimova, Uzbekistan-born, Moldova-based regional expert, told Al Jazeera.

Uzbekistan, the region’s most populous nation of 37 million, offers a perfect example.

Its iron-fisted President Islam Karimov was the first ex-Soviet leader to allow a US military base on its soil in 2001.

But four years later, he kicked it out after Washington lambasted his brutal suppression of a popular revolt in the eastern city of Andijan that killed hundreds of unarmed civilians.

In 2005, a leaked US diplomatic cable called Karimov’s daughter, Gulnara , a “robber baron” who forcibly took over lucrative businesses and was seen as her father’s successor.

As to moralising and lecturing, the tables have turned since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, observers say.

Moscow still has plenty of soft power in Central Asia – from movies and pop music to theatre festivals and propagandist TV shows that constantly lie about the war.

The Kremlin also uses its economic clout to promote the imperialist concept of the “Russian World”, where the region is seen as Moscow’s “near abroad”, and its pre-Russian heritage is snubbed as backwards and insignificant.

In 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Kazakhstan had “never had statehood”, and his ideological allies repeatedly threatened to annex its Russian-speaking northern part.

This year, Kazakhstan began extraditing Kremlin critics and supplying gas to Russia amid Ukrainian drone attacks on its oil refineries.

In January, Kremlin propagandist Vladimir Solovyov said Moscow should launch a “special military operation” – a term reserved for the war in Ukraine – in Central Asia and Armenia.

Critical remarks from minor political figures followed – but no rebukes from the halls of real power.

Meanwhile, Central Asian labour migrants have been duped or forced into enlisting to fight in Ukraine in droves, while Moscow uses Central Asian companies to import microchips, communications equipment and machine tools to build drones and missiles.

“These days, the US and Russia have switched roles. Today, it’s Russia that began building ties through moralising,” Ibragimova, the regional expert, said.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump’s administration has abandoned the pro-democracy stance and now advocates a utilitarian, transactional approach to foreign policy.

“Under Trump, the American policy in Central Asia is all about ‘just business and nothing more’, without being nosy about human rights, reforms. They are content with everything,” Ibragimova said.

Earlier this month, Trump received Saida Mirziyoyeva, the daughter of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.

A year earlier, Mirziyoyev pledged to invest up to $100bn in the US economy, buy Boeing aircraft and even US-grown cotton, even though Uzbekistan is one of the world’s largest cotton growers.

Washington did not say a word about Mirziyoyev’s crackdown on critics or his daughter’s growing domestic clout.

After largely ignoring Central Asia during Trump’s first term, the White House wants to resume its presence.

“The interest is mostly geopolitical and military-strategic, considering the region’s location in the zone of Russia’s and China’s interests,” Alisher Ilkhamov, head of the London-based Central Asia Due Diligence think tank, told Al Jazeera.

“In the future, Washington apparently wants to have a military base here as a deterrent measure against China,” he said.

The economic interests seem to be focused on rare-earth minerals – crucial for manufacturing a wide array of technology – and other critical elements, especially since China uses them as a political cudgel in its ties with Washington.

The deposits are abundant, but need development, technologies and investment.

Meanwhile, the White House shows little interest in human rights violations in Central Asia, such as the jailing of political opponents and independent journalists.

“An interest in these issues, unfortunately, is absent from Rubio’s agenda, because these problems went missing from US foreign policy priorities since Trump returned to the White House,” Ilkhamov said.

A Norwegian human rights advocate echoes his concerns.

“There are uncomfortable similarities between Trump’s worldview and established authoritarian regimes like Tajikistan and Turkmenistan,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.

“However, Marco Rubio probably has a better understanding of Central Asia and the challenges there than does [Vice President] JD Vance and [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth,” he said.

The US State Department “should bring back the focus [on human rights] if the C5+1 format is to be taken seriously going forward”, he said.

articles.title: Dem congressional candidate's police record reveals suspensions over stolen gun, insubordination
articles.summary: Johnny Garcia faced two unpaid suspensions from the Bexar County Sheriff's Office for insubordination and negligence as he runs for Texas' 35th District.
articles.body: Johnny Garcia, a candidate for Congress in Texas’ newly redrawn 35th District, faced a pair of suspensions for "job performance," "insubordination" and "conduct or action that would seriously impair job effectiveness" during his time with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office, records show. In the first suspension in 2009, Garcia brought a cellular device into a secure area against repeated instruction. The second, in 2020, arose when Garcia left a firearm in an unsecured location, where it was later stolen. In both cases, Garcia was suspended without pay. articles.title: Biden-appointed judge deals Trump another sanctuary city defeat in major immigration fight
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled Trump's lawsuit against New York City's sanctuary policies fails, citing the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine.
articles.body: A Biden-appointed judge dealt the Trump administration another legal blow Thursday, tossing its lawsuit seeking to upend New York City’s sanctuary policies after ruling that the Justice Department’s arguments amounted to a "backdoor around the Tenth Amendment." The Trump administration sued New York City in July 2025, alleging that its sanctuary laws unlawfully hinder federal immigration enforcement by restricting local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal authorities. The New York City case is one of more than two dozen lawsuits the Trump administration has filed against state and local jurisdictions over sanctuary and related policies restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities. But U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. ruled that the federal government lacked standing to challenge New York City’s restrictions on honoring ICE detainers and rejected the Justice Department’s claims that the city’s sanctuary policies are preempted by federal law. MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated the ruling in a Friday post on X, accusing the administration of attempting to turn city employees into immigration enforcement agents. "The federal government tried to turn our public servants into deportation agents and force New York City to carry out ICE’s cruel agenda. Today, a federal court rejected that effort and upheld our laws. Every New Yorker deserves to seek help from their city without fear of being targeted for deportation. We will stand by our immigrant neighbors, defend our laws and protect the promise that this city belongs to all of us," Mamdani wrote. Reyes found the administration lacked standing because striking down the city’s restrictions would not remedy its alleged harm because separate state laws restricting cooperation would remain in place. But Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and current partner at Holtzman Vogel, disputed that reasoning, arguing that the city's laws independently harm the federal government's authority regardless of whether similar state restrictions exist. "The sovereign harm is done just by the fact that New York City has the law in the books, no matter what other factors prevent practical application of the United States's position," Kambli told Fox News Digital. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS Reyes also rejected the Justice Department's argument that New York City's sanctuary policies are overridden by federal immigration law. "Even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its preemption claims fail," Reyes wrote. "All of the United States’ preemption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors." The judge pointed to the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine, which prevents the federal government from forcing state and local governments to use their own officials and resources to administer federal programs. "If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states’ constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing," Reyes wrote. Kambli, however, argued that Reyes misinterpreted the distinction between forcing local governments to assist federal immigration enforcement and preventing them from actively obstructing it. "Really what the 10th Amendment anti-commandeering means is you can't force states to go from doing nothing to affirmatively assisting. What these statutes are doing is basically preventing states from actively obstructing federal immigration enforcement," Kambli said. He argued that the Justice Department was not seeking to force New York City officials to carry out federal immigration enforcement, but instead to prevent local laws from interfering with federal authorities' ability to enforce immigration law. "That's different from the federal government saying a state or a city is required to actively assist ICE in operations," Kambli said. HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW The Justice Department also argued that New York City's sanctuary policies went beyond simply refusing to assist federal authorities by restricting information-sharing with ICE that is protected under federal law. The administration additionally claimed that the city unfairly singled out federal immigration officials for restrictions that did not apply to other law enforcement agencies. Reyes, however, found that federal information-sharing protections apply specifically to information about an individual's citizenship or immigration status and do not require local governments to provide ICE with broader details, such as a person's release date or whereabouts. "The United States’ assertion that information regarding release dates and custody status is information regarding immigration or citizenship status is contrary to law," Reyes wrote. Kambli, however, argued that the distinction over what information is being withheld misses the greater issue at hand. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "The issue is mainly whether any state or locality that prohibits cooperation is preempted by federal law, regardless of what the information is," Kambli said. articles.title: Meet the 22-year-old candidate eyeing history in key swing state as Gen Z embraces conservatism: 'Step up'
articles.summary: Dillon Fillion, a 22-year-old Domino's driver and Iowa House candidate, credits Charlie Kirk with helping Gen Z men embrace conservative principles.
articles.body: From delivering pizzas to running for an Iowa House seat, 22-year-old Dillon Fillion hopes to make history in his swing district and inspire Gen Z to embrace conservatism, which he says he's already seeing on the ground. Fillion, believed to be the youngest candidate ever to seek office in Scott County, spoke to Fox News Digital about his ambitions to cut property taxes, boost police funding, give parents more say in their children’s education and draw Gen Z to the polls. "I think people are very excited that a young person is running because they see a lot of these old people running for office, no offense to them, but people wanna see some fresh new faces and I think it's time for my generation to step up," Fillion said. Before launching his bid for the Iowa House, Fillion decided to take a gap year from Scott Community College, where he is pursuing a criminal justice degree. He currently works as a Domino’s delivery driver while hitting the campaign trail, which he described as juggling "two full-time jobs." MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP' "Basically, I do a full-time job as well as campaigning," he said. But campaigning wasn’t always Fillion’s vision. A lifelong hockey fan, he said his initial dream was to play professionally before stepping into politics. Fillion said he became interested in politics in 2019 after seeing Democrats accuse President Donald Trump of colluding with Russia, saying he found it "weird" they were "calling our president a lot of weird, untrue things." From there, he said he went down a "rabbit hole" researching what he described as corruption within the Democratic Party, which he found "baffling and shocking." "I just couldn't stand back and just watch all this stuff happen, and I decided to get involved," he said. "Keep Iowa Great!" is the slogan Fillion has plastered across campaign signs and merchandise as he works to win over Iowa voters. One of three siblings, Fillion had an upbringing "grounded in Christian family values, a strong work ethic, and the perseverance to stand by his principles no matter the challenge," according to his campaign website. Fillion credited Charlie Kirk with helping young men like him "find a purpose" and turn to conservative principles. "The men in my generation are really conservative. They admire conservative principles. I think Charlie Kirk really helped with the young men in my generation in regard to finding a purpose in life. And I think that's really helped a lot of men in my generation," Fillion said. "I do think my generation is going in the right direction in regard to conservatism. It's just, I think my generation needs to turn out more in our elections." LIZ PEEK: HASAN PIKER EXPOSES DEMOCRATS' DESPERATION TO WIN BACK YOUNG MEN Fillion will challenge incumbent Democratic state Rep. Daniel Gosa for a seat representing Iowa's 81st House District. Fillion says he finally has the opportunity to "carry the ball down the field" in his district and is calling for a leadership overhaul. "I wouldn't be in this race if I didn't think I could win it," he said. "However, my Democrat opponent does not stand up for the things that this district cares about." Among Fillion’s most high-profile endorsements are Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and Iowa House Majority Leader Bobby Kaufmann, according to his campaign website. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE One of Fillion’s top priorities is eliminating property taxes completely. His campaign website said if that isn’t "immediately achievable," Fillion will work to lower taxes as much as possible. "I wanna keep Iowa number one in affordability," he said. Crime and education are also on Fillion’s mind, and he told Fox News Digital those will be two of his top priorities if elected in November. "When I get into that legislature, I will be introducing a constitutional amendment for the Back the Blue Act to make sure our police are protected so they can do their job correctly," Fillion said. "And I will continue to empower parents and teachers in our kids' education, because parents should be the forefront of your kids' education, not the government." He said his ultimate goal is to make Iowa "the number one state to live, work, and raise a family." With voters preparing to head to the polls in November, Fillion said his campaign aims to spread more optimism and show people that Gen Z wants to make the world a better place.
