articles.title: Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia is the shortest-serving White House press secretary after a rocky tenure, but she’s not the first to go.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s latest press secretary has been let go after just five days on the job, following a widely criticised first – and only – White House news conference and amid scrutiny of her credentials.

Trump told reporters on Friday that he believed the press had been harsh towards his new top spokesperson, Katie Zacharia, but that he had advised her to “reconsider” the role.

Shortly after, Al Jazeera and other media confirmed that Zacharia would be “ transitioning out ” of the position.

That made her the shortest-serving press secretary in US history – even shorter than the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, the former White House communications director who was fired after 10 days on the job during Trump’s first term in office in 2017.

His sacking gave rise to the term “one Scaramucci” – or “a Mooch” – which journalists and White House observers use jokingly as a measure of time to predict how long Trump officials would last in their jobs. Now, a new unit of time – “one Zacharia” – is only half as long.

Recalling his own White House stint this week, Scaramucci wrote on X: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

Here’s what we know about Zacharia’s brief tenure:

Why was Katie Zacharia removed as White House press secretary?

The White House has not given an official reason for Zacharia’s departure, but it came amid mounting concerns about her competency and professional background.

During her first and only news conference on Tuesday, Zacharia appeared uneasy at the podium and struggled at times to get through her sentences. She fumbled her words while looking down at her notes, once confused the words “husband” and “president” and ended the briefing after 14 minutes, taking only three questions from reporters.

Scrutiny intensified after it emerged that Zacharia, who has a law degree and described herself as “an attorney”, had studied law at university but never passed the bar exam required to practice law in the US. She later claimed she had worked as a lawyer in China.

Conservative Fox News host Sean Hannity asked Zacharia during an awkward interview on Thursday: “Why didn’t you just say: ‘I never practised law’?”

Following news of her departure, Zacharia wrote on X that it had been “an honour” to work for Trump, calling him a “kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man”.

How was her one White House briefing received?

Zacharia, who took over from former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, was widely criticised as unpolished and unprepared during her appearance before the White House press corps on Tuesday this week, even by many of Trump’s allies.

During Hannity’s interview with Zacharia, he noted that she had been “widely panned” for her performance.

Conservative journalist and commentator Megyn Kelly said Zacharia needed “to present as a serious person”.

Jen Psaki, a former White House press secretary who worked under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, compared Zacharia’s troubled briefing to a comedy skit. “Maybe this whole White House press secretary thing isn’t really for Katie,” she said. “It’s not for everybody.”

As a fellow White House deportee, Scaramucci gave Zacharia some advice. “Speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor,” he wrote on X.

Who will take over White House press briefings now?

The White House has not announced a permanent replacement, and Trump told Fox News he is “not in a hurry” to fill the role.

The vacancy leaves Trump without a top spokesperson as the US remains mired in a conflict with Iran and heads into crucial midterm elections next month.

How many press secretaries has Trump gone through?

Zacharia was the sixth person to serve as White House press secretary under Trump. He went through four of the officials during his first term and, so far, two in his second.

Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had held the position since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025. She resigned in August to spend more time with her children.

Trump’s first-term press secretaries were Kayleigh McEnany, Stephanie Grisham, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Sean Spicer.

McEnany and Spicer now work in media. McEnany hosts several shows on Fox News, while Spicer contributing to NewsNation and has launched his own podcast.

Huckabee Sanders currently serves as the governor of her home state of Arkansas, where she is seeking re-election on November 3.

Grisham left the press secretary position after less than a year in 2020 and became First Lady Melania Trump’s chief of staff. She resigned that role after the January 6, 2021 insurrection and has since become a major critic of the US president.

Which other Trump-appointed officials have been fired?

Zacharia joins a roll call of Trump administration officials to be pushed out during his second term.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece who was previously engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr, was asked to step down from her role earlier this week after reports emerged that she offered a political donor access to senior administration officials in exchange for money.

Earlier in the year, Trump fired Attorney General Pam Bondi amid controversy over her handling of files relating to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which had become a growing political problem for the administration.

A month earlier, Trump ousted Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem , after she was grilled in Congress over a $220m advertising campaign and her comments about two US citizens fatally shot by federal officers in Minnesota .

Mike Waltz was one of the first Trump administration officials to be removed during his second term. Waltz was fired as national security adviser in early May 2025 after he mistakenly invited a journalist into a messaging application in which he and other top administration officials discussed military attack plans on Yemen.

US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle presents her credentials at the presidential palace, in Athens, Greece, November 4 [File: Louisa Gouliamaki/Reuters]

articles.title: If the Supreme Court wants to protect freedom of the press, here is its chance
articles.summary: Herridge did the right thing in protecting her sources. The justices now have a chance to protect her.
articles.body:
This month, Journalist Catherine Herridge is in the fight of her life — and the stakes for the country could not be higher. The former Fox and CBS reporter has long been one of the most prominent investigative journalists in the U.S., particularly on national security stories. She is now on her last appeal to the Supreme Court, attempting to protect the most vital prerequisite of the free press: confidentiality of sources.

At issue is a 2017 story that aired on Fox News concerning a Virginia-based training firm patronized by Pentagon officials . Herridge exposed ties of the University of Management and Technology to the Chinese military. It was the kind of difficult, complex story that made Herridge such a respected figure in her profession. The subject of the story, University of Management and Technology founder Yanping Chen, sued, claiming that the exposure had led to her loss of employment.

Such lawsuits are usually brought against journalists by disgruntled subjects under defamation or other grounds that are quickly dismissed by courts. But Chen brought a novel claim against various officials under the Privacy Act. She alleges that they disclosed to Herridge protected information about an FBI investigation. Rather than sue Herridge directly, Chen subpoenaed her to disclose the names of her sources. Herridge sat for a deposition but refused to breach confidentiality.

This is not Herridge’s first rodeo in fighting for journalistic values. Years ago, CBS News forced her out and seized her files containing confidential source information . Despite considerable costs, Herridge eventually stared down the network and forced it to return the files.

Notably, much of the Fox News story about Chen was available in the public domain. For example, a whistleblower and FBI informant had said publicly that Chen had admitted to him that she had been a colonel in China’s People’s Liberation Army. He also alleged that she told him to lie about that fact when called to testify before a federal grand jury.

Because Herridge refuses to disclose her sources, we do not know how much she actually relied on non-public information. This puts her in an impossible position: She would have to reveal sources in order to show that Chen’s claims are meritless.

In making her Privacy Act claim, Chen cited the disclosure of many facts already available publicly, including contradictions of her denials on being part of the Chinese military. The only information that had not already appeared in the public domain appears to be photographic, including a picture of Chen in a Chinese colonel’s uniform.

In this case, Herridge had the misfortune of seeking relief in Washington, D.C., where judges have been relatively permissive in allowing such disputes to go to trial. In 2023, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, an Obama appointee, tossed aside protections that other circuit courts recognize under the First Amendment. He ordered Herridge to identify her confidential sources, then held her in contempt when she refused, imposing a crippling $800-a-day fine. Even that was not enough for Chen, who tried to have the penalties increased to $5,000 a day.

Before the fines were paused in August pending appeal, Herridge had to write a check every day from her two children’s college funds. “These fines are designed to break you emotionally and professionally,” she told me. “I would walk every day to the mailbox with our oldest son for emotional and moral support.”

Unfortunately, a panel of three judges on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Cooper’s ruling. Herridge therefore went to the Supreme Court for an emergency injunction against the daily fine. The court refused to intervene immediately, although Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated that he wanted to grant the relief.

Herridge is now back before the Supreme Court, which will have a final opportunity to take the case and prevent a catastrophic blow to press freedoms. If the court again punts, then any aggrieved subject of a news story could effectively strip journalistic sources of confidentiality by alleging a Privacy Act violation.

The cause of this pileup is the highly permissive standard adopted by the D.C. Circuit for the single most important jurisdiction for investigative reporting. To compel disclosure, Chen needs only to show that the source is central to her case and that she has exhausted other avenues of discovery. This test exposes every reporter who breaks a story in Washington involving government abuse or waste. Imagine if Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein had been sued under the Privacy Act by Nixon administration officials and forced to disclose the identity of Deep Throat.

Other circuits have a balancing test that allows for a more contextual resolution of such disputes. Another approach would be to deny such compelled disclosures when the case (as here) would not likely survive a motion for summary judgment. Chen, who lost her position because of information already in the public domain, cannot possibly show meaningful injuries from these photographs.

The irony in the case is crushing. Chen is an alleged former colonel in the People’s Liberation Army, using the U.S. Privacy Act to gut a Constitutional right not recognized in China. Of course she still has rights in this country, but the question is not whether she can sue under the Privacy Act — it is what standard she must meet before the courts make a journalist betray confidential sources.

Herridge got the story right and did the right thing in protecting her sources at great personal cost. The justices now have a chance to protect her. They should take her case. Not only has it created a split among the circuit courts, but it also has a compelling record to reconsider the confusing 1972 decision in Branzburg v. Hayes , which one appellate judge ridicules for being “about as clear as mud.”

Herridge is not seeking immunity or a favor. She is a tough reporter who just wants to do her job and protect her sources under a fair legal standard. The question is whether four justices will agree and grant review in Herridge v. Chen.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution .” He previously worked for CBS News and currently works at Fox News as a legal analyst. His views do not necessarily reflect those of those networks.

articles.title: From handyman to House history: HVAC mogul Joe Strada pushes trade schools, business mindset in Florida race
articles.summary: From humbling beginnings, Joe Strada built a half-billion dollar a year HVAC business; now he wants to bring his hard work, no-nonsense approach to Washington DC.
articles.body: If Republican Joe Strada wins Florida's eleventh congressional district in three weeks, he will likely be the wealthiest individual to ever hold a seat in the US House of Representatives. It's an impressive trajectory for a man from humble beginnings who got his start fixing equipment in a bowling alley, but always had a zest for learning, building, and working with his hands. Strada, whose HVAC, electrical and plumbing company employs roughly 4,000 people across 13 states, told Fox News Digital that his journey from handyman to wealthy entrepreneur embodies the American Dream but that neither his fortune nor his business success defines him. PULLING BILLIONS FROM HARVARD TO FUND TRADE SCHOOLS? HERE’S WHAT PEOPLE ARE SAYING ABOUT TRUMP’S LATEST MOVE "How about that? Just the kid, a handyman in a bowling alley, fixing things that break…and now I'm blessed to have a business that's in 13 states, thousands of people that work for me. It's been a blessing and, I'm able to live the American dream. "But it's difficult. It was difficult with the headwinds and the rules and regulations that come out of Washington, D.C. And it was very challenging …It should be difficult, but not this challenging." Strada wants everyone to be able to benefit from the American capitalist system that brought him great success: "You know, as a business owner, I realized and recognized all the problems that Washington, D.C. is causing. All the rules and regulations that are impacting families, small business owners all across the country. And I finally said, we need a different type of person in Washington, DC. "We have enough lobbyists, politicians and attorneys there. It's time to have a business-minded person that knows how to fix things that could go to Washington, and solve problems for the real, you know, real problems for the American people." Strada is on a nationwide mission to pitch young people on the value of the trades, and suggests it's a worthy alternative to racking up massive student loans: "The word of trade is really starting to spread now. Trades people, young people just want to be successful. Sometimes they don't know there's an opportunity in the trades. You come to my company, you don't know how to spell AC, you don't know what end of the screwdriver to hold, but you're paid the very first day. We train you. We give you a career that will support yourself and your family the rest of your life. "You don't have a $250,000 student debt, and you're able to be successful… And my objective, not just with my company, it's across the country. I'm working with trade schools and high schools everywhere. I'm talking to young people all over our country to come into the trades because it's a great opportunity to live your version of the American dream." As Strada's HVAC company was growing throughout the country, a labor shortage prompted a serious challenge, and a major shift in business strategy: "The most difficult challenge was we had the opportunity to grow, and we didn't have enough labor. So I had to develop a program to teach people the trade. So we could grow, and we've been fortunate: we're in 13 states now and 4,000 people that work with us. We never would have done that if we didn't develop our own training program. "I couldn't wait for the government to come and solve my problem. I'm a business guy who solves problems and I had to go develop a training program for young people." Strada argues that people on government assistance should also take a serious look at the trades, suggesting we have a large untapped labor pool within our own borders: "The border had to be closed, and we did a great job keeping all the criminals out of our country. And as far as getting more workers, we have Americans that want to work. We have plenty of people sitting at home getting a government paycheck. Let's get them to work. "Some of them are just lazy and don't want to work, others just need the opportunity and the push to say, 'this is easy, let's get into a trade, let's learn a business.' TRUMP-BACKED GOP CANDIDATE WHO OUSTED SCANDAL-PLAGUED INCUMBENT WARNS AGAINST 'NEVER-ENDING WAR' WITH IRAN "I've have plenty of people that turned out to be an entrepreneur. They've opened their own business, and I'm very happy and gratified when I'm helping people." Hard work is at the foundation of Strada's success, and he argues an inherent part of that economic success is bringing others along: "You know, most people think when you're successful, it was handed to you. I got to tell you, David, I'm proud of the hard work my father did, but it was tough growing up. We were fortunate, we had a swimming pool, but it was mainly, a lot of times it was green because we couldn't afford chlorine. It was the best Marco Polo pool in the neighborhood. "I started with nothing. It's just hard work. The passion and drive to want to be successful, to achieve goals. And it's always about everybody wins. My employees have to win. My customers have to win, the company has to win and that's the position I like to be in is to be able to help sit at a table, moderate those kinds of things and execute those results." Ultimately, Strada downplays the importance of money, and emphasizes character, while revealing that his greatest motivation in life was born from a family tragedy: "I wake up every day the same person I was when I was 12 years old that I am today. I've been blessed to be wealthy. I worked hard. I don't apologize for it…But you know, money is just a number. My perspective is everybody puts their head on the pillow at the end of the night. And when you put your head on your pillow, what do you stand for? What's the character of who you are? "How much money you have…How many zeros you have and where the decimal point is on your bank account? None of that matters. What kind of character are you? I strive every day to do the right thing. For my God, my son in heaven who looks down at me, I want to make him proud. Every decision I make is to make him proud of me, and I do the best I can every single day." Strada's son, Joe Strada, was an innocent bystander killed by a stray bullet in Lake Mary, FL, during a gunfight outside a shopping center in 2018. Finally, Strada promises to be a powerful voice for tradeschools if he is elected to Congress next month. "Well, first of all, I would love to have my name on the SAVE Act and put it into law. That's the first thing. I also think our trade schools are so important: to treat our trade school just like we have our Ivy League colleges. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP "We're funding our Ivy league colleges billions and billions of dollars and we're graduating unhirable people that, some of them, hate America. I think the trade schools need more support from our government and treat them just like the universities." Strada will face off in the general election against Democrat James Pericola, a Clinton administration official.

articles.summary: Final site plans for President Trump’s proposed, 250-foot-tall triumphal arch do not mention the military features he previously said he would add to the project, according to documentation the Interior Department submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission. articles.body:
Final site plans for President Trump’s proposed, 250-foot-tall triumphal arch do not mention the military features he previously said he would add to the project, according to documentation the Interior Department submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission.

The president announced in late September the structure, slated to be built between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, would include a “ top grade military complex ” housing a large number of drones, snipers and ammunition. While such fortification was not part of the original proposal, Trump said it was added per the military’s “strong request.”

The latest project proposal, as shared with the planning commission, does not show any of the military features but does include other recent suggested changes — such as the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) recommended eternal flame. The D.C. planning agency is set to review the plans during its Nov. 5 meeting.

A White House official told The Washington Post on a condition of anonymity that Trump’s plans for the arch had not changed, rather, that the administration did not plan to publicly release any information about the project pertaining to national security at this stage.

The Post, who first reported on the final site plan, also cited an Interior Department spokesperson, Katie Martin, who said the current designs of the arch are capable of accommodating national security functions and more.

The Hill has reached out to the Interior Department for comment.

Trump’s plan to militarize the structure sparked concerns and criticism from lawmakers.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes Arlington, Va. — home to the National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport — criticized the plan to install a drone launching site directly in the landing path for incoming aircraft.

“Trump’s notion to make his vanity arch an ammunition depot for ‘snipers’ in a location where snipers have never been needed would place a large weapons cache within feet of thousands of tourists, pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers on major commuter traffic thoroughfares and Metro’s Blue Line,” Beyer said in a statement.

The FAA has concluded the arch would not pose a risk to airspace, according to a project evaluation published last month. Beyer argued the review did not take into account the presence of military drones.

Trump’s former national security adviser, John Bolton, called the idea to militarize the arch “not just wrong, it’s gonzo bonkers, it’s just completely divorced from reality.”

“That arch is going to be in the middle of a traffic circle. I don’t know what it’s defending against,” Bolton told MS NOW last month.

Just saying,” the former Republican lawmaker wrote on…
articles.body:
Former Rep. George Santos (R-Fla.) pitched himself on Friday to fill the vacancy left by White House press secretary Katie Zacharia.

“Hey I’m not technically open for a job because I have one already…. butttttttt… I’d jump to serve POTUS as press secretary in a heart beat. Just saying,” the former Republican lawmaker wrote on the social platform X .

A White House official announced Friday afternoon that Zacharia was “transitioning out” of her role after President Trump told reporters he advised the press secretary to “reconsider” her position.

Zacharia’s five days on the job set a new record for the shortest-serving White House press secretary.

She faced scrutiny over a shaky initial press conference , where she appeared visibly nervous, took only three reporter questions and presented herself as a lawyer on TV despite not passing the bar exam.

Santos slammed Fox News host Sean Hannity after the anchor grilled Zacharia about her legal background during a Thursday interview.

“F— you @seanhannity ! You think you are untouchable and like to sit high on your horse and judged people,” he wrote on social media .

The former lawmaker doubled down on his criticism of the Fox News host in a lengthy post on Friday evening, asking people who watched Hannity’s show to “unfollow” his X account.

“I refuse to associate with people who think that the self-righteous pig known as Sean Hannity is the standard or barometer for anything in society,” Santos wrote.

This is not the first time Santos has clashed with the Fox News host. Following his release from federal prison last fall, Hannity pressed the ex-congressman about whether he would repay the hundreds of thousands of dollars he stole to victims. Santos apologized but did not promise to pay back the amount.

Santos was expelled from Congress in 2023 and convicted on multiple counts of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. President Trump commuted his sentence last October after the ex-congressman had served three months in prison.

Since his departure from Congress, the Republican has continued to stir controversy. In August, he was issued a lifetime ban from the prediction market Kalshi after he failed to cooperate in an investigation into wagers he placed on the platform on this year’s State of the Union address.
